title: Scaling Domain Data Repetition in LLM Pretraining
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 14 Aug 2026]
    Title:Scaling Domain Data Repetition in LLM Pretraining
View PDF
            Abstract:As large language models scale, their training-token budgets must also increase to maintain an appropriate tokens-per-parameter ratio (\(\mathrm{TPP}\)). However, high-quality domain data is much harder to scale than general web data. As model size and the training-token budget increase, its fraction in the training mixture tends to decrease. Repeating the available high-quality data provides an effective way to counteract this dilution, but excessive repetition may lead to overfitting. We study this trade-off under practical LLM scaling, where the training-token budget grows proportionally with model size. For a fixed domain, we first find that, surprisingly at a fixed \(\mathrm{TPP}\), the optimal repetition count mildly increases with model size. Across different domains, we find that the optimal repetition count is strongly negatively correlated with the final validation loss of a domain: domains with lower loss can generally benefit from more repetitions. In contrast, the amount of unique domain data is only weakly related to the optimal repetition count. These findings suggest that repetition counts tuned on smaller proxy models with the same \(\mathrm{TPP}\) can provide a practical estimate for larger models.

report.summary: LLM pretraining study finds optimal domain data repetition depends heavily on validation loss, not unique data volume, and can be tuned on smaller proxy models.
report.background: Large language models require ever-growing training-token budgets to maintain an appropriate tokens-per-parameter (TPP) ratio as they scale. High-quality domain data, such as curated scientific or legal text, is much harder to expand than general web data, so its relative share in the training mixture naturally shrinks. Repeating existing high-quality examples is a practical way to counter this dilution, but too much repetition risks overfitting and degrades performance. This paper systematically studies the repetition-versus-overfitting trade-off under realistic scaling conditions, where the token budget grows proportionally with model size. The authors identify which factors actually predict optimal repetition, providing a framework for deciding how many times to repeat domain data without expensive large-scale trial-and-error.
key_points: At a fixed tokens-per-parameter ratio, the optimal number of times to repeat a domain's data actually increases mildly with model size, rather than staying constant or decreasing. This suggests larger models can absorb more repeated high-quality data without overfitting, as long as the overall token budget scales appropriately.

The strongest predictor of optimal repetition is the domain's final validation loss. Domains that reach lower loss—meaning the model learns them more easily—benefit from more repetitions, while harder domains saturate and overfit much sooner, so repeating them aggressively hurts performance.

The amount of unique domain data is only weakly related to optimal repetition. Two domains with similar dataset sizes can have very different repetition needs, indicating that data quality and learnability matter more than raw volume when deciding how often to reuse examples.

Repetition counts tuned on smaller proxy models with the same TPP can provide a practical estimate for much larger models. This makes it feasible to optimize data mixtures on small-scale experiments and transfer those settings to expensive large-scale training runs, saving significant compute.

Repeating high-quality domain data is an effective countermeasure against dilution by general web data in large training mixtures. The paper gives concrete guidance on when this strategy helps and when it becomes counterproductive, helping practitioners balance data curation and model performance.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this research offers a cost-effective way to improve domain-specific LLM performance without endlessly collecting new rare data. Training teams can run smaller proxy models to find good repetition counts, then transfer those choices to larger runs—reducing compute waste and making better use of scarce high-quality corpora. For developers, it reframes data mixing as a loss-guided decision rather than a volume-based one: measuring a domain's validation loss is more useful than counting unique tokens. For regular users, the practical benefit is stronger performance on specialized tasks like medicine, law, and code, because the model can learn deeply from limited but valuable data while minimizing overfitting.
report.tools: To explore this idea, practitioners can use data processing and curation libraries such as Datatrove for large-scale cleaning, Hugging Face Datasets for managing and repeating domain corpora, and NVIDIA NeMo for running controlled pretraining experiments. EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness helps measure validation loss across domains, and Weights & Biases can track repetition and overfitting curves to apply the paper's proxy-model tuning approach.
